current_row.boundary_rationale: Where the Aramaic sentence just before it argues from what the nations' gods did not do, this unit pivots to what Yahweh did do: a participial hymn opening, עֹשֵׂ֥ה אֶ֨רֶץ֙ בְּכֹח֔וֹ (oshb:Jer.10.12, byte), matching “God has made the earth by his power.” (web:Jer.10.12). The register shift out of the Aramaic citation formula that closed the previous verse (web:Jer.10.11) into a Hebrew creation doxology marks the edge; nothing internal to verses 12-16 breaks the hymn again. It closes on the name-formula, יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁמֽוֹ (oshb:Jer.10.16, byte) — “Yahweh of Armies is his name.” (web:Jer.10.16) — byte-identical to the same formula closing oshb:Jer.51.19, the closing verse of this hymn's twin at Jer.51.15-Jer.51.19; the wider twin pairing is held here as texture rather than as the warrant for this edge, and it does not hold at a single tier throughout — two of the five paired verses are byte-identical (oshb:Jer.10.12 and oshb:Jer.51.15; oshb:Jer.10.15 and oshb:Jer.51.18) while the other three diverge already in their consonants.
current_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this hymn into the surrounding polemic as one larger row was rejected because the participial hymn-opening and the shift out of the Aramaic citation formula are a sharper register break than anything inside the polemic itself, and the hymn is a bounded, self-closing unit with its own twin elsewhere in the book.

Those internal turns do not carry a koh-amar onset, an addressee change, or a discourse imperative of their own, so the whole stretch from the command through the report is held as one unit; the row is cut before verse 23 because that verse turns the address around, from a report about the coming danger to direct prayer speech to Yahweh.

current_row.boundary_rationale: The second person turns from Yahweh, addressed throughout the preceding complaint, onto the prophet himself: כִּ֣י אֶת רַגְלִ֥ים רַ֨צְתָּה֙ וַיַּלְא֔וּךָ וְאֵ֥יךְ תְּתַֽחֲרֶ֖ה אֶת הַסּוּסִ֑ים (oshb:Jer.12.5, byte), matching “If you have run with the footmen, and they have wearied you, then how can you contend with horses?” (web:Jer.12.5), reading as Yahweh's own reply to the complaint just voiced. The reply closes with a warning against Jeremiah's own household, אַל תַּאֲמֵ֣ן בָּ֔ם כִּֽי יְדַבְּר֥וּ אֵלֶ֖יךָ טוֹבֽוֹת (oshb:Jer.12.6, byte) — “Don't believe them, though they speak beautiful words to you.” (web:Jer.12.6) — bringing in Jeremiah's own brothers and father's house as the participants in view, אַחֶ֣יךָ וּבֵית אָבִ֗יךָ (oshb:Jer.12.6, byte), a set standing nowhere in the complaint just addressed to Yahweh. The row is cut before verse 7 because the voice there turns again, to Yahweh speaking of forsaking my house rather than replying to Jeremiah.
current_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading verses 5-6 as a continuation of Jeremiah's own complaint rather than Yahweh's reply was rejected because the addressee is named in the second person across both verses as the one who runs, whose brothers and father's house are in view — Jeremiah's own circumstances rather than Yahweh's.

A promise of compassion for Jacob and a conditional blessing for the neighbors who learn Jacob's ways are folded into the same speech rather than opening fresh units of their own — an operative judgment-oracle reading is kept for the whole four verses, with the restoration content disclosed here rather than given a separate label, since the unit opens and closes on uprooting language and the compassion clause is grammatically subordinate to it. The unit, and the chapter, close on the closing-speech formula, נְאֻם יְהוָֽה (oshb:Jer.12.17, byte), matching “says Yahweh.” (web:Jer.12.17), the clause immediately before it reading, “But if they will not hear, then I will pluck up that nation, plucking up and destroying it,” (web:Jer.12.17); a fresh command opens immediately afterward at web:Jer.13.1, corroborating the close read here.
current_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the restoration promise in verses 15-16 out of the judgment envelope that opens and closes the unit was rejected because that promise is grammatically subordinate to the uprooting announced in verse 14, introduced by after I have plucked them up rather than by any independent formula.

current_row.boundary_rationale: A new address opens at 13:20, though not immediately in the feminine singular: “Lift up your eyes, and see those who come from the north” (web:Jer.13.20) renders שאי שְׂא֤וּ עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ וראי וּרְא֔וּ הַבָּאִ֖ים מִצָּפ֑וֹן (oshb:Jer.13.20, byte tier), a doubled-note verse whose two opening imperatives each carry a ketiv/qere pair -- feminine singular on the ketiv, masculine plural on the qere -- with the intervening object עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ taking a masculine-plural suffix under either reading. The feminine-singular Jerusalem address itself begins only with לָ֔ךְ and תִּפְאַרְתֵּֽךְ later in the same verse, and governs from there through the closing vocative at 13:27, distinct from the king-and-queen-mother pair addressed just before. The sustained indictment of Jerusalem-as-woman runs through the scattering sentence (13:24-25) and the uncovering of her skirts (13:26) to the closing apostrophe: “Woe to you, Jerusalem” (web:Jer.13.27), where א֥וֹי לָךְ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם (oshb:Jer.13.27, byte tier) is the oy lexeme (sweep: 8 verses book-wide) -- a different word from the bare hoy, ה֣וֹי (oshb:Jer.22.13 and oshb:Jer.23.1, byte tier), that opens the woe oracles at 22:13 and 23:1; the vav-prefixed shape, וְה֣וֹי (oshb:Jer.22.18, byte tier), stands here and, in its own pointing, again at 34:5 (sweep: 2 verses), both funeral cries, so this row is not typed woe_oracle. The span’s own divine formula is the neum-YHWH at 13:25, נְאֻם יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Jer.13.25, byte tier), not a koh-amar: the chapter’s four koh-amar sites, 13:1, 13:9, 13:12 and 13:13, all stand before this row opens.
current_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Joining 13:20-27 to the preceding royal oracle (13:18-19) into one ten-verse row was considered: the shift from the royal pair's plural address to the feminine-singular Jerusalem address that governs from mid-13:20 is real, but the two share the same humiliation-and-exposure imagery, so the fold-together reading is not unreasonable.

current_row.boundary_rationale: “This is Yahweh’s word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought” (web:Jer.14.1) renders the full header, אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֤ה דְבַר יְהוָה֙ אֶֽל יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ עַל דִּבְרֵ֖י הַבַּצָּרֽוֹת (oshb:Jer.14.1, byte tier) -- the OAN/topical-header shape, attested at four sites book-wide (sweep: 4 verses: 14:1, 46:1, 47:1, 49:34). The header is kept with the drought description that follows (14:2-6: mourning gates, dry cisterns, cracked ground, the doe forsaking her fawn, the wild donkeys panting) rather than standing alone: no addressee or scene shift separates the title from what it introduces, and at the other three sites the same header shape carries its own attached content rather than standing bare -- 46:1 heads the whole nations collection, while 47:1 and 49:34 each head a single-nation oracle with its own attached setting. Framed here as judgment_oracle by its dominant content -- a report of covenant devastation already unfolding -- rather than superscription, since only one of the six verses is the bare title.
current_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating 14:1 as its own one-verse superscription row, separate from the drought description, was considered and set aside in favor of the larger bundled unit, since the description carries the row's substance and no addressee shift separates the header from what it introduces.
current_row.literature_type_guess: topical word-event header opening a drought-devastation report

current_row.device_notes: Jer.14.3, inside the span, carries one note in the separate single-witness ketiv/qere inventory, the unpointed ketiv צעוריהם beside the pointed qere צְעִירֵיהֶ֖ם (oshb:Jer.14.3, byte tier). Jer.13.27, just before this row, carries a petuchah (single-witness, tier-3 WLC corroboration in the Prophets); no verse within 14:1-6 itself carries a parashah mark.
